newsitem.title: EGYPT: Mideast investors focus on basics of making money.
newsitem.headline: Mideast investors focus on basics of making money.

text.p: The good news for the Middle East is that investors are increasingly ignoring its political instability to see whether they can make money here.
The bad news from the three-day Middle East/North Africa Economic Conference, ending on Thursday, was that the region is still making it hard for those seeking a good enough return.
The biggest change in the region's fortunes came in May with the election of a right-wing Israeli government that slammed the brakes on the Middle East peace process.
But fears this could sever investment flows were disproved in Egypt, the largest Arab stock market open to foreign investors.

"It was really surprising -- nothing happened. In fact investment accelerated as international investors could see that Egypt was not necessarily affected by the peace process," said Mohamed Taymour, chairman of brokers Egyptian Financial Group.

Bankers estimate that Egypt's surging stock market, buoyed by an ambitious privatisation programme, will have sucked in up to $600 million out of the $850 million invested by foreign investors in Arab stock markets in 1996.
But ING Barings stock analyst Angus Blair said the region's share of portfolio investment in the world's emerging markets would still remain "shockingly low" at less than one percent.
The International Monetary Fund estimates that little has changed either regarding direct foreign investment in regional companies or projects.

Middle East and North African countries typically attract annual inflows equivalent to 0.5-0.75 percent of gross domestic product. An Asian economy like Malaysia, by comparison, drew nine percent in the peak year of 1992 and six percent last year.

But IMF officials were keen to stress repeatedly at the conference that there had been a dramatic change recently in attitude in the region to "structural reform" -- revamping economies with deregulation, privatisation and competition.
"Everybody recognises this change and everybody recognises that this change will unleash huge potential," said Mohamed El-Erian, deputy director of the IMF's Middle East department.
Countries in the region may have recognised that they were falling behind by not opening to the increasingly global economy but few have yet made it easier for foreigners to do business.
"There have not been many significant changes on foreigners' access to these markets," said ING's Blair. "Those that were open are still open, those that were closed remain closed."
Many countries still set limits on foreign ownership while at the same time asking for more international investment.

Tariff barriers still stifle trade, with even Arab states barely trading with each other. Intra-regional trade accounts for only seven percent of their total trade compared with around 60 percent in the European Union.
Arabs admit the region's instability has left a legacy of suspicion that hardly eases foreign investment flows.
"They think the investor comes to exploit them and then leaves," said Mahmoud al-Jarwani, executive president of the Muscat Securities Market in Oman.
"So it may take some time to get a clear vision of this region's dealings with foreign investors," he added.
